title: Aspect outside the indicative

objectives.can: Say what the choice of present, aorist or perfect stem contributes in an infinitive, participle, subjunctive or imperative.

explanation.summary: Outside the indicative, the present, aorist and perfect stems do not say when something happens. They say how the speaker looks at it: in progress, as a whole, or as a resulting state. Reading an imperative, an infinitive, a participle or a subjunctive well means asking why this stem was chosen.

sections.heading: Three ways of looking at an action
body: Grammarians call the difference between the stems 'aspect'. The present stem views an action in progress or as a process: ongoing, repeated, or habitual. The aorist stem views it as a whole, from outside, without saying how long it lasted or whether it was repeated. The perfect stem views a state that results from an earlier action: the door is open, the thing is written, the person is favoured.

In the indicative the stems also carry time. The aorist indicative usually refers to the past. Outside the indicative this link is weak or absent. An aorist imperative is not a command about the past, and an aorist subjunctive after ἵνα does not look back. The stem tells you the speaker's view, and the time comes from the sentence and its context.

View of the action
Typical effect
Not to be confused with

a single act, or an act simply stated

sections.heading: Imperatives and subjunctives
body: A command can be given with either stem. In Romans 6:13 Paul writes μηδὲ παριστάνετε, a present imperative with a negative, and then ἀλλὰ παραστήσατε, an aorist imperative of the same verb. Many readers take the present to speak of a continuing practice and the aorist of a decisive act of handing oneself over. That is a tendency in how the stems are used, not a rule that fixes the sense of every instance.

The same holds for the subjunctive after μή or ἵνα. In John 15:8 the present subjunctive φέρητε, 'that you keep bearing', stands beside the aorist γένησθε, 'and become'. The first looks at a continuing activity, the second at a thing that comes about. The negative commands of the New Testament are often a present imperative or an aorist subjunctive, as in Mark 5:36 and Matthew 1:20, but the pattern is not absolute, and it is wrong to read it as 'stop doing' for the present and 'do not even begin' for the aorist. The context decides whether anything had begun.

sections.heading: Infinitives
body: The infinitive shows the same contrast. In Philippians 1:21 the present infinitive ζῆν, 'to live', is set against the aorist infinitive ἀποθανεῖν, 'to die'. Living is seen as a process, dying as an event. In Luke 18:1 the present infinitive προσεύχεσθαι goes with πάντοτε, 'always': it suits an activity that is meant to go on.

In Romans 12:1 the aorist infinitive παραστῆσαι asks the readers to present their bodies, seen as one act. The stem does not say that the act is single or that it happens only once, and it does not say when: the time of an infinitive is set by the verb it depends on.

sections.heading: Participles: time is a tendency
body: A participle has a stem and a case, but no time of its own. Its time is relative to the main verb, and context settles it. Two tendencies are useful. An aorist participle often names something that happened before the main verb, or at the moment of it: in Acts 16:27 the jailer saw the doors, drew his sword, and then was about to kill himself. A present participle often names something going on at the same time as the main verb: in Matthew 1:20 the angel appeared while saying something, ἐφάνη … λέγων.

These are tendencies. An aorist participle can be at the same time as its verb, as in 'answering, he said' (ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν), where the answering and the saying are one event. The perfect participle names a state: κεχαριτωμένη in Luke 1:28 describes the person as one on whom favour has been bestowed, with that favour still true now. When the time is not obvious, read the sentence and not only the stem.

sections.heading: The perfect outside the indicative
body: The perfect stem is rarer outside the indicative, and each case is worth noticing. In Mark 4:39 Jesus tells the sea πεφίμωσο, a perfect imperative: 'be in a state of being muzzled', and the sea then goes still. In Acts 16:27 the jailer thinks that the prisoners are in the state of having escaped, ἐκπεφευγέναι, a perfect infinitive. In Matthew 10:26 κεκαλυμμένον is a perfect participle: what is covered up. In each case the perfect shows a state, not an event.

misunderstandings: Taking the aorist outside the indicative as 'past'. An aorist imperative, infinitive or subjunctive does not refer to the past; the participle is only often prior to the main verb.

Treating the present imperative as meaning 'keep on' and the aorist as 'do it once' in every case. These are tendencies. Many present imperatives simply give a command, and many aorists cover repeated acts.
Reading the perfect as 'past and over'. The perfect looks at a state that holds as a result, and the state is what the speaker cares about.

Looking for a different English tense for each stem. The stems often make no difference in English translation. The aim is to see why the author chose this stem, not to find a translation that shows it.

deeper.heading: Why some verbs prefer one stem
body: Some verbs, by their meaning, are used more often in one stem. Verbs of dying, finding or arriving describe events and tend to appear in the aorist. Verbs of being, living or remaining describe states and tend to appear in the present. When an author uses the unexpected stem, the choice can be meaningful, but a single verse seldom proves it. Look for a pattern across a passage before building an argument on one form.

examples.analysis: The same verb in two stems. παριστάνετε is a present imperative, negated by μηδέ: do not go on presenting. παραστήσατε is an aorist imperative, after ἀλλά: present yourselves. Neither form refers to a time; the contrast is between a continuing practice and a decisive act, which is the usual way these stems are read.

examples.analysis: Two infinitives in two stems. ζῆν is present, 'to live', and ἀποθανεῖν is aorist, 'to die'. Living is seen as a process and dying as an event. Both are articular infinitives, used as nouns, and neither has a time of its own.

examples.analysis: Four forms from three stems. ἐνθυμηθέντος is an aorist participle in a genitive absolute: the thinking comes before the angel's appearance. ἐφάνη is the main verb. λέγων is a present participle, saying something as the angel appears, at the same time. φοβηθῇς is an aorist subjunctive in a prohibition, 'do not be afraid', with no reference to the past.

examples.analysis: Participles and an infinitive of three stems. γενόμενος, ἰδών and σπασάμενος are aorist and come before ἤμελλεν. νομίζων is a present participle, going on as he draws the sword. ἀνεῳγμένας is a perfect participle, 'standing open', the state of the doors. ἐκπεφευγέναι is a perfect infinitive: he thought that the prisoners had escaped and were gone.

practice.prompt: παριστάνετε (word 1) and παραστήσατε (word 10) are the same verb as imperatives. What do their stems tell you?

options: The first speaks of a continuing practice and the second of a decisive act, as the stems are usually read
Both are present; the second is only an emphatic spelling
The first is about the past and the second about the future
They are two different verbs that happen to look alike
practice.explain: The present stem views an action as a process and the aorist views it as a whole. This is a tendency in usage. Neither imperative refers to a time. The first option mistakes the stems for tenses of time.

practice.prompt: In this verse ζῆν (word 3) is present and ἀποθανεῖν (word 7) is aorist. What is the difference?

options: Dying is future and living is past
Living is seen as a process and dying as an event
Living is certain and dying is possible
Only the present infinitive is a real infinitive
practice.explain: The present stem looks at an activity in progress. The aorist looks at an event as a whole. The infinitives have no time of their own, so the tenses are not 'now' and 'then'. Certainty is not what the stems express.

practice.prompt: In this verse φέρητε (word 9) is present and γένησθε (word 11) is aorist. Both follow ἵνα. What does the choice of stems add?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: φέρητε views the bearing of fruit as continuing; γένησθε views becoming disciples as a whole
Nothing at all: the two stems are interchangeable
φέρητε is passive and γένησθε is active
φέρητε is past and γένησθε is future
practice.explain: In the subjunctive the stems mark aspect, not time. The present suggests an ongoing activity and the aorist a thing viewed as a whole. 'Nothing at all' is too strong: authors choose a stem for a reason, even when English cannot show it.

practice.prompt: σπασάμενος (word 12) is aorist and νομίζων (word 18) is present. How are they likely to relate in time to the main verb ἤμελλεν (word 15)?

options: Both are simultaneous with it, because participles never express time
σπασάμενος is future and νομίζων is past
σπασάμενος is probably before it and νομίζων goes on along with it
Both come after the main verb
practice.explain: An aorist participle often names an act before the main verb, and a present participle an activity at the same time. These are tendencies, and context confirms them here: he draws the sword, then is about to act, still supposing the prisoners had gone.

practice.prompt: Σιώπα (word 9) is a present imperative and πεφίμωσο (word 10) is a perfect imperative. What does the perfect add?

options: A plural subject
A request for a resulting state: be muzzled, and stay so
A question rather than a command
A command about the past
practice.explain: The perfect stem views a state that results from an act. Here it asks for a lasting condition. It is still a command, directed at the future, so it is not about the past.

check.prompt: φοβηθῆτε (word 2) is an aorist subjunctive after μή. Does the aorist make this a prohibition about the past?

options: Yes: the aorist always refers to the past
Yes, because μή changes the time
No: it is a command for the future, and the aorist is the speaker's way of viewing the fear as a whole
No: it is not a prohibition but a question
check.explain: Outside the indicative the aorist does not mark past time. This is a negative command about what the hearers should do. The verb is aorist because the fear is seen as a whole, not because it is past.

check.prompt: ἐνθυμηθέντος (word 3) is an aorist participle and λέγων (word 11) a present participle. How do they relate to ἐφάνη (word 9)?

options: Both happen after the angel appears
The thinking is probably before the appearing, and the saying goes on as the angel appears
The thinking is future and the saying is past
Both are exactly simultaneous with it, with no difference between the stems
check.explain: An aorist participle often names something prior to the main verb; a present participle often names something going on at the same time. Both are tendencies that the context here supports.

check.prompt: κεχαριτωμένη (word 6) is a perfect participle. What does the perfect stem say about the person addressed?

options: That she is doing something right now
That favour was once given and is now over
That she is in a state of being favoured, a result that holds
That she will be favoured in the future
check.explain: The perfect stem views a resulting state. It is not a simple past: the first option makes the favour finished and gone, and the perfect speaks of a state that still holds.

check.prompt: προσεύχεσθαι (word 8) is a present infinitive with πάντοτε (word 7), 'always'. Why does the present suit it?

options: The aorist infinitive is not allowed after δεῖν
The present stem makes the infinitive refer to the present moment
Because the verb is deponent
Praying is seen as a continuing activity, and 'always' fits that view
check.explain: The present stem views an action as a process or a habit. The infinitive does not mark time, so the first option mistakes the stem for a time. The aorist is not forbidden here.

check.prompt: παραστῆσαι (word 9) is an aorist infinitive. What is its stem most likely contributing?

options: That the readers must never do it again
That the presenting is seen as a whole, as one act
That the presenting happened in the past
That the act is impossible
check.explain: The aorist views an action as a whole, from outside. It does not say that the act happened before the main verb (παρακαλῶ asks for something still to come) or that it happens only once.

check.prompt: ἐκπεφευγέναι (word 19) is a perfect infinitive after νομίζων. What does the jailer suppose?

options: That the prisoners should have escaped
That the prisoners will escape in the future
That the prisoners are in the state of having escaped
That the prisoners are escaping at this moment
check.explain: The perfect stem views a resulting state: for the jailer the prisoners have got away and are gone. A present infinitive would have viewed the escape as in progress.

check.prompt: Both μεθύσκεσθε (word 2) and πληροῦσθε (word 9) are present imperatives. What does the present suggest about the commands?

options: They concern a continuing pattern of life
They are about what happens at this very moment
They refer to the past
They concern a single occasion
check.explain: A present imperative often gives a command for a continuing or habitual way of living. That is a tendency, not a rule, but it fits this contrast between a way of life and its opposite. A single occasion would more naturally use the aorist.

check.prompt: ἁμάρτητε (word 7) is an aorist subjunctive after ἵνα μή. What time does it refer to?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: Future time only, because every subjunctive is future
Past time: the readers have already sinned
No time of its own: the writer's aim concerns what they may do from now on
Present time only, since γράφω is present
check.explain: The aorist subjunctive does not mark past time. The time of the sinning is set by the sentence: the purpose is something the writer hopes for. A subjunctive often looks ahead, but the context sets the time.

reading.why: Romans 6 sets present and aorist imperatives side by side (6:12–13, 6:19). The same writer's choice of stems is easy to see.
